title: Egyptian riddles and Mosaic myths
source_text: Πλὴν καὶ ἄκων ἐνέπεσεν ὁ Κέλσος εἰς τὸ μαρτυρεῖν τῷ νεώτερον εἶναι τὸν κόσμον καὶ οὐδέπω μυρίων ἐτῶν εἰπὼν καὶ Ἕλληνας ταῦτα νομίζειν ἀρχαῖα, ὡς πρεσβύτερα διὰ τοὺς κατακλυσμοὺς καὶ τὰς ἐκπυρώσεις οὐ τεθεωρήκασιν οὐδ᾿ ἀπομνημονεύουσιν. ἔστωσαν δὲ τῷ Κέλσῳ τοῦ περὶ τῶν ἐκπυρώσεων καὶ ἐξυδατώσεων μύθου διδάσκαλοι οἱ κατ᾿ αὐτὸν σοφώτατοι Αἰγύπτιοι, ὧν τῆς σοφίας ἴχνη ἄλογα ζῷα προσκυνούμενα καὶ λόγοι παριστάντες εὔλογον εἶναι καὶ ἀνακεχωρηκυῖάν τινα καὶ μυστικὴν τὴν τοιαύτην τοῦ θεοῦ θεραπείαν. κἂν μὲν Αἰγύπτιοι περὶ τῶν ζῴων σεμνύνοντες ἑαυτῶν τὸν λόγον θεολογίας φέρωσι, σοφοί εἰσιν· ἐὰν δὲ ὁ τῷ Ἰουδαίων συγκαταθέμενος νόμῳ καὶ νομοθέτῃ πάντα ἀναφέρῃ ἐπὶ τὸν τῶν ὅλων δημιουργὸν μόνον θεὸν. ἥττων εἶναι παρὰ Κέλσῳ καὶ τοῖς ὁμοίοις αὐτῷ λογίζεται τοῦ μὴ εἰς λογικὰ μόνον καὶ θνητὰ ζῷα ἀλλὰ καὶ εἰς ἄλογα κατάγοντος τὴν θεότητα ὑπὲρ τὴν μυθικὴν μετενσωμάτωσιν. τὴν περὶ τῆς πιπτούσης ἀπὸ τῶν ἁψίδων τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ψυχῆς καὶ ἕως τῶν ἀλόγων ζῴων, οὐ μόνον ἡμέρων ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀγριωτάτων. καταβαινούσης. καὶ ἐὰν μὲν Αἰγύπτιοι μυθολογῶσι, πιστεύονται πεφιλοσοφηκέναι δι᾿ αἰνιγμῶν καὶ ἀποῤῥήτων, ἐὰν δὲ Μω(??)σῆς ὅλῳ ἔθνει συγγράφων ἱστορίας καὶ νόμους αὐτοῖς καταλίπῃ. μῦθοι κενοὶ νομίζονται μηδ᾿ ἀλληγορίαν ἐπιδεχόμενοι οἱ λόγοι αὐτοῦ·
pass_a_gloss: Nevertheless even unwilling (ἄκων) Celsus fell into (ἐμπίπτω) bearing witness that the world is rather young (νεώτερος) and not yet of ten thousand years, having said that the Greeks too consider these things ancient (ἀρχαῖα), because older things, on account of the deluges and the conflagrations, they have not beheld (θεωρέω) nor remember (ἀπομνημονεύω). Let there be (ἔστωσαν) for Celsus as teachers (διδάσκαλος) of the myth (μῦθος) about the conflagrations and inundations (ἐξυδάτωσις) the Egyptians, wisest according to him, of whose wisdom the traces (ἴχνη) are irrational animals (ἄλογα ζῷα) being worshipped (προσκυνέω) and arguments (λόγοι) presenting that such service (θεραπεία) of God is reasonable (εὔλογος) and withdrawn/recondite (ἀνακεχωρηκυῖα) and mystical (μυστικός). And if Egyptians, magnifying (σεμνύνω) their own doctrine about the animals, bring theologies (θεολογίαι), they are wise; but if the one who has assented (συγκατατίθεμαι) to the law and lawgiver of the Jews refers (ἀναφέρω) everything to the craftsman of all, the only God, he is reckoned (λογίζομαι) by Celsus and those like him inferior (ἥττων) to the one who brings down (κατάγω) the divinity (θεότης) not only into rational (λογικός) and mortal animals but also into irrational ones, beyond (ὑπέρ) the mythical transmigration (μετενσωμάτωσις), that about the soul falling (πίπτω) from the vaults (ἁψίς) of heaven and descending (καταβαίνω) even to irrational animals, not only tame (ἥμερος) but also most savage (ἄγριος). And if Egyptians mythologise (μυθολογέω), they are believed to have philosophised through riddles (αἴνιγμα) and secret things (ἀπόρρητα); but if Moses, writing for a whole nation, leaves them histories and laws, his words are considered empty myths (μῦθοι κενοί) not even admitting (ἐπιδέχομαι) allegory (ἀλληγορία).
pass_b_english: Yet Celsus, even against his will, fell into bearing witness that the world is rather young and not yet ten thousand years old, when he said that the Greeks too consider these things ancient because, owing to the floods and conflagrations, they have neither seen nor remember anything older. Let the Egyptians, whom he counts the wisest, be Celsus’s teachers of the myth of conflagrations and inundations. The traces of their wisdom are irrational animals that are worshipped, and arguments to show that such worship of God is reasonable, and of a hidden and mystical kind.

If the Egyptians, to give dignity to their doctrine about the animals, offer theological explanations, they are wise. But if one who has assented to the law and the lawgiver of the Jews refers everything to the Creator of the universe, the only God, he is counted by Celsus and those like him inferior to one who brings divinity down not only into rational and mortal living beings but even into irrational ones. This goes beyond the mythical doctrine of transmigration, which tells of the soul falling from the vaults of heaven and descending as far as irrational animals, not only tame ones but even the most savage. And if the Egyptians tell myths, they are believed to have philosophized through riddles and secrets; but if Moses, writing for a whole nation, leaves them histories and laws, his words are thought to be empty myths that do not even admit of allegory.

choices.choice: Staged Greek shows '(??)' inside Μωϋσῆς and its cases (Μω(??)υσῆς, Μω(??)σέως): an encoding artefact for the diaeresis, no textual effect. The chapter's last clause runs on into 1.21 ('τοῦτο γὰρ Κέλσῳ καὶ τοῖς Ἐπικουρείοις δοκεῖ'), which the staged rows place at the head of 1.21; it is translated there. 'ἔστωσαν' read as concessive ('Granted, then, that ...'). 'ὑπὲρ τὴν μυθικὴν μετενσωμάτωσιν, τὴν περὶ τῆς πιπτούσης ... ψυχῆς' taken as: bringing the divine into beasts goes even beyond the Platonic myth of transmigration, which itself is described by the apposition. The 'vault of heaven' and the falling soul echo Plato, Phaedrus 246c–248c (ὑπουράνιος ἁψίς, 247b); Origen does not name Plato here, so no inline classical citation is added. 'θεότης' rendered 'divinity' (reviewer change from 'Godhead', which carries a Trinitarian sense not present here). Celsus's remark about the Greeks is in indirect speech (εἰπὼν ... νομίζειν), so it is not set in quotation marks. No Scripture quoted.
καὶ ἄκων: 'Celsus too fell, against his will' -> 'Celsus, even against his will, fell' (καί goes with ἄκων, not with Celsus)
οὐ τεθεωρήκασιν οὐδ᾿ ἀπομνημονεύουσιν: 'have not seen or remembered' -> 'have neither seen nor remember' (keeps the present tense of the second verb)

ἔστωσαν ... διδάσκαλοι: 'Granted, then, that ... are the Egyptians, the wisest of men in his view' -> 'Let the Egyptians, whom he counts the wisest, be Celsus's teachers' ('of men' was added; 'then' had no Greek word)
ἀνακεχωρηκυῖάν τινα καὶ μυστικήν: 'and something recondite and mystical' -> 'and of a hidden and mystical kind' (agrees with θεραπείαν, plainer word)
θεότης: 'the Godhead' -> 'divinity' (pagan practice degrading the divine; 'Godhead' carries Trinitarian weight not in the Greek)
ἀπὸ τῶν ἁψίδων: 'vault' -> 'vaults' (plural as in the Greek)
